Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

a willing horse needs no spur phrase

also a fast-running horse needs no spurs

classical

Cic. Phil. 3.19: sed tamen currentem, ut dīcitur, incitāvī (Lewis & Short s.v. incitō)

currentem incitāre

Literally “to urge on one who is already running”, of a person who needs no urging. Cicero marks it as a saying with ut dīcitur; so too currentem hortārī (Cic. Att. 5.9.1, Lewis & Short s.v. currō).

Other words

  • currentī calcāria addere

    also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 1.8.1: addere calcāria sponte currentī (Lewis & Short s.v. calcar)

    Literally “to put spurs to one who is running”.

  • Equō currentī nōn opus calcāribus.

    also used · modern · Traupman 256

    Literally “a running horse needs no spurs”. Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase. It is made from the classical saying.

SourcesJohn C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency.

Cicero, Philippics 3.19, and Pliny, Epistulae 1.8.1, checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (12 November 2026).

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
